name: Guanidinoacetate methyltransferase (GAMT) deficiency
aliases: creatine deficiency due to GAMT deficiency

clinicalPearls: One of three cerebral creatine deficiency syndromes; an autosomal recessive defect of the second and final step of creatine biosynthesis, which converts guanidinoacetate to creatine.
Unique among the group in causing accumulation of neurotoxic guanidinoacetate as well as cerebral creatine depletion, making it the most clinically severe of the three.
Typically presents in infancy or early childhood with global developmental delay, intellectual disability and treatment-resistant epilepsy.
An extrapyramidal movement disorder (dystonia, chorea, athetosis or ballismus) with globus pallidus/basal ganglia signal change on MRI is characteristic.
Brain proton MR spectroscopy shows a strikingly depleted or absent creatine peak, a useful non-invasive clue shared across the whole group.

The biochemical hallmark is markedly raised guanidinoacetate in plasma and urine with low creatine, distinguishing it from AGAT deficiency (low guanidinoacetate) and transporter deficiency (normal guanidinoacetate).

Treatable: oral creatine supplementation combined with dietary arginine restriction, ornithine and sodium benzoate to lower guanidinoacetate; pre-symptomatic treatment can prevent neurological injury.
Increasingly identified by newborn bloodspot screening for elevated guanidinoacetate, allowing treatment before symptom onset.
reference.pathophysiology: GAMT (guanidinoacetate methyltransferase, encoded on chromosome 19p13.3) catalyses the second, final step of creatine synthesis, transferring a methyl group from S-adenosylmethionine onto guanidinoacetate (GAA) to form creatine. Biallelic loss-of-function variants produce a dual insult: deficiency of creatine and phosphocreatine, which are central to cellular energy buffering in high-demand tissues such as brain and muscle, and accumulation of the immediate precursor guanidinoacetate. Cerebral creatine depletion impairs neuronal energy homeostasis and underlies the developmental delay and regression. Accumulated guanidinoacetate is proconvulsant and neurotoxic, interacting with GABA-A receptors and contributing to basal ganglia injury and the extrapyramidal movement disorder; this toxic accumulation explains why GAMT deficiency is more severe than AGAT deficiency, in which no such intermediate builds up. Because endogenous synthesis is blocked at the terminal step, treatment aims both to replace creatine and to suppress guanidinoacetate production.
additionalDifferentials: AGAT deficiency and creatine transporter (SLC6A8) deficiency, the other cerebral creatine deficiency syndromes
Glutaric aciduria type 1 and other organic acidaemias with basal ganglia injury and movement disorder
Mitochondrial disorders presenting with encephalopathy and extrapyramidal signs
Neurodegeneration with brain iron accumulation and other basal ganglia disorders causing dystonia
Non-syndromic intellectual disability and autism spectrum disorder
additionalInvestigations: Plasma and urine guanidinoacetate and creatine/creatinine (raised guanidinoacetate, low creatine)
Brain proton MR spectroscopy (depleted or absent creatine peak)
Brain MRI (globus pallidus and basal ganglia signal abnormality)
GAMT enzyme activity in cultured fibroblasts or lymphoblasts
Newborn bloodspot guanidinoacetate screening where available
redFlags: Treatment-resistant epilepsy with developmental delay or regression in infancy
Emerging extrapyramidal movement disorder with basal ganglia signal change
Delayed recognition of a treatable disorder, risking irreversible neurological injury
reference.prognosis: With early, ideally pre-symptomatic, treatment neurodevelopmental outcome can be near-normal. Once established, the intellectual disability, epilepsy and movement disorder respond only partially and largely persist.
pitfalls: Plasma creatine may be only mildly reduced and easily overlooked; guanidinoacetate is the more reliable diagnostic marker.
MR spectroscopy creatine depletion is shared by all three syndromes and cannot distinguish them; biochemistry and genetics are required.
Routine metabolic screens (plasma amino acids, acylcarnitines) are typically normal, so specific guanidinoacetate measurement must be requested.
Assuming the disorder is untreatable like transporter deficiency; GAMT deficiency responds to therapy and must be actively sought.
references: Cerebral creatine deficiency syndrome consensus guidance
management: Replenish cerebral creatine stores with oral creatine monohydrate supplementation, the mainstay of disease-specific therapy
Reduce accumulation of neurotoxic guanidinoacetate through an arginine-restricted diet combined with ornithine supplementation, adding sodium benzoate where needed
Control the treatment-resistant epilepsy with antiepileptic drugs, guided by EEG characterisation
Manage the extrapyramidal movement disorder (dystonia, chorea, athetosis) symptomatically
Monitor biochemical and neurological response with serial plasma and urine guanidinoacetate and creatine and with brain proton MR spectroscopy
Initiate treatment pre-symptomatically wherever possible, prompted by newborn screening or an affected sibling, to preserve neurodevelopment
Coordinate care across metabolic medicine, neurology and dietetics, with genetic counselling and sibling testing for this autosomal recessive disorder
